selected.title: A landslide sent a tsunami 1,580 feet up an Alaska mountainside
selected.summary: A newly reported study describes an August landslide-triggered tsunami in Alaska’s Tracy Arm fjord. Water and debris surged 1,580 feet up the opposite slope, underscoring the risks of fast-changing glacier landscapes.
selected.why_it_matters: As glaciers retreat and slopes destabilize, remote fjords may pose sudden hazards to tour boats and other visitors. Better monitoring and warning systems could make a difference.
selected.challenge_question: How high did the Alaska tsunami surge up the mountainside?
selected.answer_explanation: The reported run-up was 1,580 feet (481 meters) up the mountainside. The study links the wave to a landslide in Tracy Arm fjord.
selected.butterfly_question: How could glacier retreat change the risks faced by people visiting remote fjords?

selected.title: Anthropic says it will direct 5% of its shares to a public-benefit fund
selected.summary: Anthropic announced a plan to commit 5% of its shares to a fund for public-benefit initiatives. The proposal raises questions about how AI-generated wealth might be shared and how such a fund would be governed.
selected.why_it_matters: If implemented, the commitment could offer a high-profile model for directing some technology-company value toward public causes, while testing how corporate pledges translate into lasting benefits.
selected.challenge_question: What share of Anthropic’s shares did it say it would commit to a public-benefit fund?
selected.answer_explanation: The reported commitment is 5% of the company’s shares. The announcement describes a planned commitment; its eventual value and distribution depend on implementation and future share value.
selected.butterfly_question: Who should benefit when a powerful technology creates enormous private wealth?

selected.title: China names its first researchers for grants that can last 15 years
selected.summary: Nature reports that China has selected the first researchers for a long-term grant program that begins with five years of funding and can be extended for another ten. The design contrasts with shorter grant cycles common in many research systems.
selected.why_it_matters: Longer funding horizons may give researchers more room to pursue uncertain questions, but their effects on discovery and scientific careers will take time to assess.
selected.challenge_question: How long could the new Chinese research grants last, including extensions?
selected.answer_explanation: The program starts with a five-year grant that can be extended for another ten years, for a potential total of 15 years.
selected.butterfly_question: Would longer research grants produce better discoveries—or concentrate opportunity among fewer scientists?
